title: Arrow grammar: the three legal arrows, one simple case each
intent: After this scene the learner can say: "An arrow starts on electrons (a lone pair or a bond). Bond → atom breaks a bond and makes a lone pair (H–Cl → H⁺ + Cl⁻); lone pair → atom makes a new bond (HO⁻ + H⁺ → H₂O); bond → new bond moves a π pair into a new bond (ethylene + H⁺ → CH₃CH₂⁺)."

reagent.label: three separate cases, one arrow each

products.name: H⁺ and Cl⁻ (arrow 1)
products.note: The H–Cl bond pair becomes a fourth lone pair on Cl.

products.name: water (arrow 2)
products.note: A lone pair of HO⁻ becomes the new O–H bond.

products.name: ethyl cation (arrow 3)
products.note: The π pair becomes a new C–H bond; the other carbon is left with a +.

beats.caption: Arrow 1, bond → atom. In water, H–Cl gives up H⁺. Cl pulls the shared pair harder, so H is δ+.

arrows.why: Bond → atom: the H–Cl pair goes onto Cl, the atom that pulls harder. The bond is gone and Cl has a fourth lone pair.

beats.caption: The H–Cl pair moves onto Cl. The bond breaks: Cl keeps the pair as Cl⁻, and H is left bare as H⁺.
Arrow 2, lone pair → atom. Hydroxide, HO⁻, has three lone pairs on O. H⁺ has no electrons at all.

arrows.why: Lone pair → atom: a pair on O, the rich site, goes to H⁺, the poor one, and becomes the new O–H bond.

beats.caption: One lone pair of O becomes a new O–H bond. HO⁻ + H⁺ → H₂O: the − and the + cancel. Nothing breaks.
Arrow 3, bond → new bond. Ethylene’s π pair sits above and below the C=C: electron-rich. H⁺ is poor.

arrows.why: Bond → new bond: the π pair, the rich site, becomes a new C–H bond to H⁺. C2 drops to three bonds and a +.

beats.caption: The π pair leaves the C=C and makes a new C–H bond. The other carbon lost its share: it is now C⁺.
The grammar: start on electrons (dots or a line); end on an atom, or where a new bond forms.

stereoCallout.title: No stereo here
stereoCallout.text: Nothing in this scene is a stereocentre: it is about grammar only. Each arrow changes one bond or one lone pair, and the charges follow from the electron count.

quiz.q: Which of these arrows is NOT legal?

options.text: An arrow that starts on H⁺ and points at a lone pair of HO⁻.
options.why: Yes. H⁺ has no electrons to send. Arrows start at electrons: the lone pair of HO⁻ goes to H⁺.

options.text: An arrow from the H–Cl bond onto Cl.
options.why: That is legal (bond → atom): the pair becomes a lone pair on Cl and the bond breaks. It is arrow 1 of the scene.

options.text: An arrow from the C=C π bond to H⁺, making a new C–H bond.
options.why: That is legal (bond → new bond): the π pair becomes the new C–H bond. It is arrow 3 of the scene.

notes: Redone 2026-10-20 (novice review #6): each arrow kind is shown on the simple case Lesson 08 has the learner draw (s07 HO⁻ + H⁺, s08 H–Cl, s09 ethylene + H⁺), in the same order as the grammar list of s06 after the first case. The earlier allyl chloride version had Cl leave on its own and a resonance shift, too much for a first picture.
